# Museum Accessibility Evaluation Guide
**Researched 5 September 2026 from live, publicly accessible pages (no login, subscription or payment required)**

## How to use this guide
The core principle: **accessibility is not a single property of a museum.** It varies by gallery, by exhibition, by programme, by day of the week, and by who you are. Every museum below has a general accessibility statement — and every one of them also has specific galleries, times or visitor groups that statement does not cover. Check at the level you'll actually be visiting.

---

## Part 1 — The 13-point evaluation checklist

Work through these before booking. Record "not stated" rather than guessing — a gap in a website is itself a finding worth acting on.

| # | Domain | Ask specifically |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Physical access** | Is *every* entrance step-free, or only one? Which one? |
| 2 | **Navigation** | Are there named galleries with **no** lift or level access? Is there a published step-free route/map? |
| 3 | **Seating** | Do benches have **backs and armrests**? In which rooms? Can you borrow a stool? |
| 4 | **Tactile** | Which *specific objects/rooms* can be touched? Guided or self-guided? Booking notice? |
| 5 | **Audio description** | Live tours, recordings, or both? Where hosted? Does it need an app/account? |
| 6 | **Captions** | Are *all* gallery films captioned, or only those made after a certain date? |
| 7 | **Sign language** | Pre-recorded videos, or live interpreters? Live = for programmes only, or gallery visits too? |
| 8 | **Accessible interpretation** | Large print — all exhibitions or only some? Easy read? Braille? |
| 9 | **Sensory** | Is there a quiet room, is it *dedicated* or multi-use, and is it open at all times? |
| 10 | **Assistive equipment** | Wheelchairs/scooters/ear defenders — how many, and what notice? |
| 11 | **Staff support** | Will staff *push* a wheelchair? Operate a lift? Escort an assistance dog? |
| 12 | **Digital information** | Visual story, downloadable map, communication cards, website accessibility statement? |
| 13 | **Advance planning** | What is the longest booking lead time, and is the booking line open at weekends? |

---

## Part 2 — Five worked museum profiles

### British Museum (London) — *britishmuseum.org/visit/accessibility-museum*

**Strong, museum-wide:** 153 free audio descriptions (SoundCloud, no account needed); 200+ BSL videos with English captions, free on YouTube; detailed third-party AccessAble access guide.

**Gallery- or exhibition-specific only:**
- **Touch tours exist in two galleries only** — Room 4 (Egyptian sculpture, 9 highlight objects) and Rooms 18/18b (Parthenon, 12 stops). Guided touch tours require **two weeks'** notice via `groups@britishmuseum.org`.
- **Large print** covers *all paid* exhibitions but only *some free* exhibitions, plus eight named galleries.
- **Induction loops** are at a small number of fixed desks, not throughout the galleries.

**Documented limitations — read these carefully:**
- **Captions appear only on AV displays produced after September 2020.** Older films may have none.
- **Galleries with no lift or level access:** Room 16 (Bassae), Room 67 (Korea), Room 69 (Greek and Roman Life), Room 95 (Chinese Ceramics).
- Lifts are described as "**most** … are wheelchair accessible" — not all.
- Loan wheelchairs are limited and need **two working days'** notice, and the box office is **closed at weekends and bank holidays** — so a Saturday visitor must book by Thursday.
- **The Museum states it cannot provide staff assistance around the Museum for wheelchair users.** A chair is lent; nobody pushes it.
- Seating is in selected galleries and is "mostly benches and stools," with backed seating only in selected galleries.

> This single museum disproves the "ramp = accessible" assumption on its own: it has excellent remote resources, four inaccessible galleries, uncaptioned older films, and no pushing assistance.

---

### V&A South Kensington — *vam.ac.uk/info/disability-access*

**Museum-wide:** large print in most galleries and **all** exhibitions; free companion/carer ticket; BSL-and-subtitled welcome video; visual story; 13 accessible toilets.

**Limited or conditional:**
- **The Tunnel entrance is not wheelchair accessible.** The V&A describes itself as "an old building that has been added to over the years," with accessible routes in different parts.
- **Nearest step-free Underground station is Knightsbridge, about 0.6 miles away** — South Kensington itself is not step-free. This is a journey-planning fact most museums omit.
- **Subtitles: only "a selection" of gallery films.** The V&A states it is "working to subtitle all videos" — an honest admission of incompleteness.
- **Assistive technology is confined to the National Art Library and the Prints & Drawings Study Room** — not the galleries.
- **Quiet Space** (Level 2, Rooms 73/74a) is multi-use and **may not be available during every Friday Late.**
- **No Changing Places toilet on site** — nearest is the Science Museum.
- Only **two sets** of child ear defenders. Wheelchairs need 24 hours' notice.
- Tactile resources are tied to particular galleries, not general.

---

### Smithsonian (Washington DC) — *si.edu/visit/VisitorsWithDisabilities*

**Baseline:** "at least one entrance is accessible" at each museum — a minimum, not a guarantee of full access. Aira service available.

**Programme-tied, not general:**
- Tactile/verbal description tours and sign language interpretation require **two weeks'** notice.
- Assistive listening and interpretation are offered "upon request for **all public programs and scheduled tours**" — i.e. attached to organised events, not to walking in and browsing.
- **"Morning at the Museum"** sensory-friendly access is a **monthly, pre-registered programme at one museum**, not a museum-wide offer.
- **The Smithsonian states plainly that its museums do *not* offer dedicated hours or early opening for neurodiverse visitors by request.** This is exactly the kind of explicit negative statement worth looking for.
- "See Me at the Smithsonian" serves adults with dementia — a cognitive-access programme, again by registration.
- The site notes individual museums *may* offer additional resources — so the central page cannot be assumed to describe any specific museum.

---

### Sir John Soane's Museum (London) — *soane.org/visit/accessibility*
**The historic-building case study — and a model of honest disclosure.**

The museum opens by stating it is a **Grade I listed, 19th-century building, so "access isn't always straightforward."** It then lists the constraints rather than hiding them:

- Everything is on open display and visitors are asked **not to touch anything** — so tactile access is genuinely unavailable here, unlike at the British Museum.
- **Historic furniture cannot be sat on**; you must ask staff for a seat.
- Uneven flooring, floor grilles you can see through, **dark and narrow areas**, extremely fragile objects.
- **Very little artificial light** — daytime visits advised; torches or extra overhead lighting sometimes available on request.

**Physical access — unusually precise:**
- Internal *and* external platform lifts provide step-free access, but **24 hours' notice is required** (020 7405 2107) because **the Grade I listing means the lift cannot be sited in a public space** and staff must operate it.
- **Wheelchairs wider than 41cm, deeper than 84cm or higher than 82cm cannot pass the corridors** — visitors must transfer to the museum's custom-built narrow wheelchairs.
- Crutches and walking sticks are fine "everywhere inside," but **some spaces are too narrow for walking frames.**
- Guide dog policy developed with the Guide Dogs Association; **a staff member must accompany you and your dog**, so you must call ahead.
- **Induction loops at the front desk and shop only** — plus loops set up for seated lectures on request.
